transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, thank you. Um... well, it’s honestly a little embarrassing to admit out loud, but I guess that’s why I’m here. I’ve just been having this issue with... well, with eating, I suppose. 

My schedule is pretty chaotic right now because I’m taking some college classes, but I’m also working as a financial manager. Which, you know, is a lot of responsibility and stress for someone my age, so I’m always juggling a million spreadsheets and deadlines during the day. By the time I get home, my brain is just completely fried. And what made me finally come in today is that, after work or after my classes are done, I’ll get back to my place, open up my laptop just to zone out for a bit, and I end up eating... just an unbelievable amount of food. 

Like, I’ll get a whole takeout meal, which should be enough for dinner, right? But I’ll finish all of that, and then I’ll immediately start on a big bag of chips, and then I feel like I need something sweet, so I’ll eat whatever sweets or chocolate I have around the kitchen. I’ll even start rummaging through my desk drawer for all those random little study snacks and granola bars I keep in there, just eating whatever I can find. 

It’s way, way more than I ever actually planned on having when I first sat down. I always tell myself I'm just going to have dinner. And the crazy part is, I would absolutely never eat like that around anyone else. If I’m out with friends or if someone is just in the room with me, I eat a completely normal amount. But when I'm alone with my laptop, it just turns into this huge mountain of food, and it's really starting to bother me.
After these episodes of eating a large amount of food, do you ever try to compensate for it by making yourself vomit, using laxatives, fasting, or exercising excessively?

No, no, I don't do anything like that. I know some people do, like, I had a roommate freshman year who would go to the gym for literally three hours if she ate a slice of pizza, but I don't do that. Honestly, after I eat all that food, I just feel so incredibly full and sluggish that the idea of exercising is just... impossible. I couldn't even if I wanted to. I just sit there feeling terrible about myself. 

And I definitely don't make myself throw up or take anything. I actually have a really big phobia of throwing up—emetophobia, I think it's called? Ever since I was a little kid and had this awful stomach bug on a family road trip to Florida, I've been terrified of it. So even though I feel so uncomfortably full, like my stomach is stretched tight like a drum, I just kind of suffer through it. 

I don't really fast either, because with my schedule, I have to be sharp. If I'm looking at financial projections for work and I haven't eaten all day, my blood sugar drops and I get the shakes, and I can't focus on the numbers. And then I have my college classes on top of that, so I have to eat during the day just to function. So no, I don't try to undo it or anything... I just carry all that guilt and all that food with me the next day, which just makes me feel even worse about the whole thing.

latest_inference.note: The patient reports recurrent episodes of eating a large amount of food in a discrete period of time, often when alone, followed by feelings of guilt and distress. There is no evidence of compensatory behaviors such as purging, fasting, or excessive exercise, which rules out bulimia nervosa (F50.20) and anorexia nervosa (F50.00). The pattern is not better explained by another specified or unspecified eating disorder, narrowing the diagnosis to binge-eating disorder (F50.81).

inference_history.note: The patient presents with behaviors suggestive of excessive eating, particularly in private and in association with stress, which raises suspicion for a possible eating disorder. However, further information is needed to distinguish between specific eating disorder subtypes and to assess for other contributing factors such as mood or anxiety disorders.
